newsitem.title: USA: Wired's future seen uncertain after IPO withdrawal.
newsitem.headline: Wired's future seen uncertain after IPO withdrawal.

text.p: Wired Ventures is likely to undergo a shakeup after it pulled its initial public offering of stock for a second time this year, according to market analysts.

Goldman Sachs, lead underwriter for the offering, said on Friday the initial public offering for the company, which publishes Wired magazine, had been withdrawn. The offering was put on hold on Thursday evening, the day before the new issue was to debut on the public market.

Before it was withdrawn, the offering had been reduced to 3 million from 4.75 million common shares and the price range was slashed to $8 to $10 a share from $12 to $14, according to a source close to the underwriters.
Still, a number of analysts and investment professionals said the deal was overpriced, even after the reduction.
The IPO was postponed for the first time in July amid a broad decline in high-technology and Internet stocks.

Wired said in a statement released late Friday that the decision to pull the deal for the second time "was based solely on market conditions, particularly as they pertain to Internet-related companies."
"The company further said that speculation in the media on other reasons behind the decision was incorrect," Wired said.

News reports had speculated that distribution on the Internet of an internal memorandum from Wired Ventures Chief Executive Louis Rossetto may have been a factor in the withdrawal, since Wired was in a "quiet period" surrounding its IPO, as mandated by the Securities and Exchange Commision.
The memo was first reported on Thursday on the web site of a New York-based financial online service, which said it had also been posted on The Well, a San Francisco based Internet discussion group.

Although Wired magazine accounts for more than 90 percent of Wired Ventures' revenues, the company had been building up its HotWired site on the World Wide Web and analysts saw this as an attempt to capitalise on higher valuations achieved by Internet companies that had gone public earlier this year.
It also markets an Internet search engine called HotBot.

But the market for Internet IPOs has chilled significantly since the meteoric performance of companies such as Netscape Communications Corp. in August 1995 and of Yahoo! Inc. this year, and analysts said many investors saw Wired more as a traditional publishing concern in any case.
Analysts now expect the company to reshuffle it's HotWired unit, perhaps sharply reducing its staffing, which they said has swelled to be among the biggest for an Internet publisher.
"HotWired is deadweight, from a business perspective," said one analyst, who said the company might have been more successfully priced had it spun off as purely a magazine.
Wired is likely now to seek to make a private placement, or perhaps seek venture funding, rather than to return to the public market after two high-profile withdrawals, analysts said.
Wired, formed in late 1992, had been posting heavy losses.

Last week the company said in documents filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission that total revenues for the first nine months of 1996 were $25.1 million, up from $16.7 million in the year-earlier period.

But the company's net loss swelled by more than ten-fold to $42.0 million from the prior-year nine months, including a writeoff of $20.5 million for in-process research and $6.4 million in stock options-related compensation expense.
At Sept. 30, the company had cash of nearly $4 million, but a working capital deficit of $6.8 million and an accumulated deficit of $36.8 million.
Prior to the offering, Wired Ventures had a shareholders' deficit of $448,000, according to the documents.
"There was nothing to indicate that they would be markedly improved," one of the analysts said. "As far as the IPO is concerned, it's a business, not an editorial crusade."
